name: Overhead Desk
summary: A 90° top-down desk film: printed dashboards swept away by a hand, the Acme mark set down on the drop, a finger tapping Roll back on a phone notification.
look: Warm wood desk with soft top light, paper printouts, sticky notes, a coffee cup, a phone and a laptop seen straight down; flat illustrated hands with drop shadows; rig label and frame guides as camera annotations.

components.name: Desk surface
components.role: warm wood with grain; the stage every object is dropped onto

components.name: Printed dashboards
components.role: paper sheets with charts, the physical form of “too many dashboards”

components.name: Hands
components.role: stylised pointing hand with a drop shadow; the human in the loop

components.name: Phone notification
components.role: the anomaly as a push notification with Roll back / Acknowledge

components.name: Brand coaster
components.role: the Acme mark as an object that gets placed on the desk on the drop

components.name: Rig label + frame guides
components.role: OVERHEAD RIG · 90° tag and corner guides that name the camera

motion.name: Object drop
motion.how: each object enters from off-frame (y ±300 px) with back.out(1.6) in 0.35 s and a shadow that tightens as it lands; one object per beat at 120 BPM

motion.name: Hand sweep
motion.how: one arc move 0.5 s (power3.inOut) that pushes the papers out left with 6 px motion blur, finishing on the drop

motion.name: Tap
motion.how: finger dips 8 px (scale 0.97) in 0.08 s on the downbeat, button ripple 0.4 s expo.out, phone shake ±4 px for 0.2 s when the notification arrives

story: Hook: a desk buried in printed dashboards, “How many dashboards did you check today?”. Reveal: a hand sweeps the papers away and sets the Acme Pulse card down on the drop. Proof: the phone buzzes with “Checkout conversion −18% since 09:42 after deploy #2231” and a finger taps Roll back. CTA: a tidy desk, laptop showing “You ship. Pulse watches.” and Start free.
adapt: Print your users’ current tools as paper sheets for the hook, and show your product’s key moment on a phone or laptop lying on the desk. Real overhead footage of hands with a screen-replaced phone works just as well as illustration.

references.note: the overhead (bird’s-eye) shot and how it is used
top-down 90° framing and flat-lay use in product video

fit.risk: Top-down desk shots are warm and human but a little generic; illustrated hands must be very well drawn (or real footage) or the frame looks cheap, and the phone UI has to stay big enough to read at 1:1.
